questionText: What does a directory primarily map?
options: Memory pages to scheduling priorities
Passwords to plaintext copies
Names to file-system objects or identifiers
CPU registers to instruction opcodes
explanation: A directory organizes name lookup; the object's metadata can be stored separately, such as in an inode.

questionText: What distinguishes an absolute path from a relative path?
options: It starts from the filesystem root rather than the current directory
It always refers to a larger file
It must identify a device driver
It cannot contain directory names
explanation: Absolute paths are interpreted from the root; relative paths use a current starting directory.

questionText: What is a file descriptor in a UNIX process?
options: A process-local handle used for an open file or related I/O object
The complete contents of a file
A permanent file name valid in every process
The physical disk platter number
explanation: Descriptors index process-managed open-object references used by operations such as read and write.

questionText: What does an open file's current offset usually track?
options: The user's password length
The count of all directories on disk
The position used for the next sequential read or write
The physical CPU core number
explanation: Sequential I/O advances an offset in the open file description, subject to operation semantics.

questionText: Which value is file metadata rather than file content?
options: A pixel in a stored image
A sample in a stored audio stream
Last-modification timestamp
The first paragraph of a document
explanation: Metadata describes attributes of the object rather than the application's stored payload.

questionText: What does directory search/execute permission normally allow in UNIX?
options: Rewrite all directory entries without write permission
Read every file's contents automatically
Traverse the directory to resolve known entry names
Execute every file inside regardless of file permissions
explanation: Directory search permission enables path traversal; listing and modifying entries require other permissions.

questionText: What does a symbolic link store conceptually?
options: A path to another location
The target's complete CPU execution state
A mandatory second copy of all target data
A guarantee that the target cannot disappear
explanation: A symbolic link is resolved by interpreting its stored path and can become dangling if the target is removed.

questionText: What does mounting a filesystem do?
options: Change all file owners to the current user
Attach its directory tree at a mount point
Copy every file into CPU registers
Erase its free-space map
explanation: Mounting makes another filesystem's hierarchy accessible through the namespace.

questionText: A regular-file read reaches the end with no more bytes available. What return value conventionally indicates EOF in UNIX read()?
options: The file's inode number
A new positive file descriptor
Always minus 1
0 bytes
explanation: A zero-byte read result indicates EOF for a regular file; a negative result indicates an error.

questionText: Why open a file with read-only access when no writes are needed?
options: Force the file to occupy one block
Request only the needed access and prevent writes through that descriptor
Make the file impossible for any user to modify forever
Guarantee all reads bypass the page cache
explanation: Open access mode limits operations through the handle and supports least-privilege use.

questionText: What does a block bitmap commonly indicate?
options: Which filesystem blocks are free or allocated
Which CPU instruction runs next
Which process owns every register
Which user typed each key
explanation: One bit per allocation unit provides a compact free-space map.

questionText: What is the immediate namespace effect of unlinking a file name?
options: That directory entry is removed
Every open descriptor to the file is instantly invalidated
All other hard links are automatically removed
The disk must be securely overwritten immediately
explanation: Unlink removes one name; object lifetime also depends on other links and open references.

questionText: What does a regular file's logical size describe?
options: The count of users who can read it
Always exactly the physical allocated block count times block size
The byte range of its content as seen by applications
The number of CPU cores used to create it
explanation: Logical size and physical storage allocation can differ because of holes, allocation rounding or metadata.

questionText: Why does an OS cache recently read file data in RAM?
options: Guarantee the file can never be modified
Reduce repeated storage I/O and latency
Remove the need for all permission checks
Replace the directory tree permanently
explanation: Cached data can satisfy later reads without another storage transfer, while consistency rules still apply.

questionText: Does a file-name extension alone reliably enforce a file's actual format or safety?
options: Yes; an extension encrypts the file
No; it is a naming convention, not proof of contents
Yes; the OS verifies all data whenever a name changes
No; files can never have extensions
explanation: Applications and security checks must inspect or validate content rather than trusting a suffix alone.

questionText: A 9000-byte file uses 4096-byte blocks without holes. How many data blocks are needed?
explanation: Ceiling(9000/4096)=3; two blocks hold only 8192 bytes.

questionText: A 9000-byte file occupies three 4096-byte blocks. How many allocated data bytes are unused?
options: 1288 bytes
808 bytes
3288 bytes
4096 bytes
explanation: Allocated capacity is 12288 bytes; subtract 9000 to obtain 3288 bytes of final-block slack.

questionText: What advantage does indexed allocation have over traversing a linked list of data blocks for random access?
options: It needs no metadata storage
Every file must be physically contiguous
Block pointers can be looked up through an index
It makes all file offsets zero
explanation: Indexed structures locate a target block through metadata rather than reading each preceding data block in a chain.

questionText: What is an extent?
options: A password-validation routine
The number of CPUs in the machine
A mandatory one-byte file
A run of contiguous blocks described compactly
explanation: Storing a starting block and length can represent many contiguous blocks with one record.

questionText: Why do conventional UNIX filesystems normally disallow user-created hard links to directories?
options: Hard links always duplicate the entire directory contents
Directories cannot have identifiers
Only files with extensions have metadata
They can create cycles and complicate directory-tree invariants
explanation: Restrictions maintain tractable parent relationships and namespace traversal, aside from special system-managed entries.

questionText: A symbolic link points to a path that is removed. What commonly remains?
options: A full copy of the target data appears automatically
Every parent directory is deleted
The symlink exists but resolution of its target fails
The symlink becomes a guaranteed hard link
explanation: A symbolic link stores a path, not a reference that necessarily keeps the target object alive.

questionText: Why can a simple atomic rename generally not move a file directly between different filesystems?
options: The operation crosses independent metadata and storage domains
Rename requires no metadata changes
Both filesystems must have identical file contents
A file name cannot contain letters
explanation: Cross-filesystem moves are typically implemented using copy and removal rather than one ordinary within-filesystem rename.

questionText: A process keeps a descriptor open after the file's last name is unlinked. What usually happens?
options: It can keep accessing the object until the last open reference closes
The descriptor must immediately become a different user's file
Every read must return unrelated data
The OS instantly reuses the data blocks despite the open reference
explanation: Namespace removal and object lifetime are separate; open references keep the object alive.

questionText: How can a file's logical size exceed the bytes allocated to its data blocks?
options: Directories store all missing bytes as text
The file has negative-size blocks
Every extra logical byte must reside in a CPU register
Unwritten holes can represent zero ranges without allocated data blocks
explanation: Sparse allocation records holes, so logical offsets can exist without storing a physical block for each range.

questionText: What does a correctly implemented atomic append-position selection help prevent?
options: Every crash-related data loss
Concurrent writers choosing the same old end offset before separate writes
Any need to check write return values
Every possible interleaving within arbitrary multi-write records
explanation: Append mode associates each write with the current file end atomically for supported filesystem semantics; record framing still matters.

questionText: A write requests 1000 bytes but returns 600 without error. What should code needing all bytes do?
options: Continue appropriately with the remaining 400 bytes
Assume all 1000 were written
Delete the file immediately
Resend all 1000 without tracking progress
explanation: Short writes are possible; robust code advances the buffer and retries the unsent portion while handling later errors.

questionText: Why is close() alone not a universal guarantee that recent file data survives sudden power loss?
options: Storage devices contain no volatile state
Buffered writes may still need an explicit persistence operation
Every close synchronizes every filesystem on the machine
Closing always erases user data
explanation: Persistence requires the relevant fsync-style operations and storage guarantees, not merely releasing the descriptor.

questionText: What does metadata journaling primarily help recover after a crash?
options: Every application's latest unsaved document by definition
The exact pre-crash CPU register values
Filesystem metadata consistency
Passwords forgotten by users
explanation: A journal supports coherent metadata updates; application data durability depends on the mode and explicit persistence protocol.

questionText: Why should data blocks generally be initialized before exposing a new file mapping that references them?
options: To make every write use the same physical block
Because directories cannot be modified after data writes
Avoid exposing stale or uninitialized block contents
To remove the need for ownership checks
explanation: Ordered update protocols prevent reachable metadata from pointing to inappropriate residual data.

questionText: A filesystem has 32768 allocation blocks. How many bytes are required for a one-bit-per-block bitmap?
options: 4096 bytes
32768 bytes
262144 bytes
1024 bytes
explanation: 32768 bits divided by 8 bits per byte equals 4096 bytes, excluding headers or replication.

questionText: With 4096-byte blocks and 4-byte block pointers, how many pointers fit in one indirect block?
explanation: An indirect block holds 4096/4=1024 pointers when all bytes are available for entries.

questionText: A user may write a file but lacks write permission on its parent directory. What does this distinction generally imply?
options: The user can always rename every neighboring entry
Content modification may be allowed while deleting its name is not
The file's contents must be immutable
Writing the file automatically grants directory ownership
explanation: File write rights govern data; directory write/search rights govern namespace updates, with additional policy such as sticky bits possible.

questionText: For requested permission mode 0666 and umask 0027, what mode results using requested AND NOT umask?
explanation: Clearing masked bits removes group write and all other-user rights: 0666 & ~0027 = 0640.

questionText: Why can directory indexing help a directory containing many entries?
options: Guarantee all names hash to different values
Make every file consume one disk sector
Eliminate all access checks
Reduce the work needed to locate a named entry
explanation: Hashes or tree indexes avoid an exhaustive linear scan for typical lookups, while collision and consistency handling remain.

questionText: Why should a privileged program avoid blindly following an attacker-controlled symbolic link while creating a sensitive file?
options: Following a link cannot change path resolution
Symbolic links always contain encrypted data
A link's name proves its target owner
The path may resolve to an unintended protected target
explanation: Secure path-resolution and handle-based operations are needed to avoid redirecting privileged file operations.

questionText: Ten small files each use one 4 KiB data block. Ignoring metadata, how much block space do they allocate?
options: 10 KiB
4 KiB
400 KiB
40 KiB
explanation: Each independent file consumes one block under these assumptions: 10×4=40 KiB.

questionText: An inode has 12 direct pointers and one single-indirect pointer. Blocks are 4 KiB and pointers 4 bytes. Ignoring other limits, how many data blocks can these address?
explanation: The single-indirect block holds 4096/4=1024 pointers; adding 12 direct pointers yields 1036 data blocks.

questionText: A double-indirect pointer uses 4 KiB pointer blocks and 4-byte pointers. How many data blocks can that pointer address?
explanation: Each of two pointer levels fans out to 1024 entries; 1024²=1048576 data blocks, excluding pointer-block overhead.

questionText: For a local filesystem with suitable guarantees, why might a durable replace protocol write and fsync a temporary file, rename it, then fsync the parent directory?
options: Because fsync on a file always persists every directory change
To prevent all future edits to the file
Because rename always copies the complete file contents
Persist both the new contents and the namespace update
explanation: File sync covers content; directory sync makes the changed name association durable, subject to filesystem and device guarantees.

questionText: Why should recovery not replay an incomplete journal transaction as if it were committed?
options: Incomplete transactions necessarily contain no metadata
Replay automatically invents missing writes
It could expose only part of a logically related metadata update
Every journal entry is independently an entire filesystem
explanation: Commit records and ordering distinguish completed atomic update groups from interrupted partial records.

questionText: Why must a copy-on-write tree update preserve a path of new metadata before publishing its new root?
options: New blocks contain no references
Root publication automatically fixes all partially initialized descendants
The old tree must be modified in place before every read
Readers of the old root must still see a coherent old tree
explanation: Constructing a coherent new path before root switch provides a consistent transition while preserving referenced old versions.

questionText: Two separate open() calls access the same inode. Must their sequential offsets be shared?
options: No; regular files never use offsets
Yes; an inode has exactly one global offset
Yes; all descriptors in the machine share one offset
No; separate open file descriptions normally have independent offsets
explanation: Object identity and open-description identity differ; separate opens normally track separate positions, unlike dup or inherited shared descriptions.

questionText: For a single-indirect data access with no relevant caches, assume the inode is already in RAM. How many disk-block reads locate and read the target data?
explanation: One read obtains the indirect pointer block and another reads the selected data block; inode and directory reads are excluded by assumption.

questionText: Why might deleting a file fail to immediately free all its physical blocks in a snapshotting filesystem?
options: A snapshot may still reference those blocks
All deleted data is automatically overwritten before unlink returns
Snapshots contain only file names and no references
Deletion necessarily allocates a new full copy
explanation: Reference-aware reclamation retains blocks needed by surviving snapshots or clones.

questionText: Why is a filesystem checksum insufficient by itself to guarantee recovery of corrupted data?
options: Detection does not provide a correct replacement copy
All checksum algorithms encode every original bit redundantly
A checksum is always larger than its file
Checksums prevent every hardware fault
explanation: Recovery needs redundancy, backups or another source of valid data; integrity detection alone cannot reconstruct arbitrary damage.
